To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
host shifts are a common cause of reproductive isolation and that host shifts have caused speciation.
host shifts are common, and that host shifts can and do initiate insect speciation.

(1) a host shift has absolutely initiated insect speciation in eight cases; (2) in 26 cases, a host shift has contributed to the evolution of new barriers to gene flow, and in 43 cases, a host‐associated genetic difference has been detected; and (3) in 26 of the cases where a host shift has led to the evolution of a new reproductive barrier, there is evidence that the host shift initiated speciation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of host shifts and host‐associated speciation (HAS) in the diversification of the insect order Lepidoptera.
the role of host shifts and speciation in insects.
understanding the processes that generate biodiversity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

“host shifts initiate insect speciation,” but we are not yet at that point, and the phrase “host shifts can initiate insect speciations” is a more appropriate statement of the current state of knowledge.
host shifts can and do initiate insect speciation.
a host shift can initiate speciation, but it is not clear whether it does so frequently.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
host shifting is a common mechanism for initiating speciation in insects, but it is not a necessary one.
host shifts are a common and important driver of insect speciation.
host shifts have played a role in speciation in 51% of the systems reviewed here, with a subset of those systems supporting the hypothesis that host shifts have initiated speciation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
host shifts can be an important mechanism of sympatric and allopatric speciation.
the role of host shifts as an initiating force in speciation has not been adequately tested and deserves more attention.
the hypothesis that host shifts initiate insect speciation should be considered as one possible cause of insect speciation and not dismissed as a rare event.
